text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Psychiatry consultation to confirm the diagnosis, advise on an SSRI at OCD doses with buprenorphine, plan exposure and response prevention, and advise on how his staff can stop carrying out rituals for him
  • Opioid review under the CDC 1943 guideline: benefits and harms reviewed with him, a prescription drug monitoring program check before every controlled-substance prescription, urine drug testing with consent and explained as part of care, one prescriber and one pharmacy, a nonjudgmental DSM-5-TR assessment for opioid use disorder, and no abrupt stop of codeine
  • Buprenorphine with naloxone for opioid use disorder and pain: induction in the clinic at one week after about 20 hours without codeine, then 8 mg twice daily, dispensed weekly at first; naloxone nasal spray at home; no benzodiazepines; leftover codeine to a pharmacy take-back
  • Pain after major trauma: scheduled acetaminophen up to 3,000 mg a day, physical therapy for the chest wall, left shoulder and low back, graded activity, sleep, and pain coping skills woven into his therapy; no NSAID long term
  • OCD treatment: exposure and response prevention with a psychologist, weekly 90-minute sessions with home practice, then twice weekly; sertraline from 50 mg, raised every four to six weeks as tolerated toward 200 mg; response judged by the Y-BOCS at each visit; augmentation with a low-dose antipsychotic (aripiprazole or risperidone) or a switch to clomipramine considered only if the response is poor after 8 to 12 weeks at the highest tolerated dose
  • Accommodation by staff: with his written consent, his assistant joins two therapy sessions; staff stop carrying out rituals for him in planned steps that follow his exposure hierarchy, offer support instead of reassurance, and are not asked to report on him
  • Safety: a structured safety assessment, a written safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in his phone, means safety for opioids, and safety review at every visit
  • Hearing: audiometry, then hearing aids and a remote microphone if hearing loss is confirmed; hearing protection when flying and in the factory
  • Nutrition and weight: a dietitian visit, three meals a day built into his exposure plan (food made by his cook, then food from a restaurant), weight at each visit, albumin at baseline and follow-up; no supplements needed
  • Kidney health: creatinine, eGFR and urine albumin at baseline and a metabolic panel at follow-up while on scheduled acetaminophen and any new medicine; acetaminophen kept at or below 3,000 mg a day; no long-term NSAID
  • Privacy: care documented in the clinic record only; letters about his health go only to people he names

resource.title: Howard Hughes synthetic care plan
resource.description: Obsessive-compulsive disorder in a wealthy and powerful 41-year-old aviator and businessman with chronic pain after a near-fatal plane crash and long-term codeine use. The episode covers a Y-BOCS severity rating, DSM-5-TR criteria with the insight specifier and the differential (obsessive-compulsive personality, illness anxiety, post-traumatic stress after the crash, psychosis); a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; exposure and response prevention as first-line therapy with an SSRI (sertraline, raised to 200 mg) at OCD doses under the APA 1928 guideline and its 1934 watch and NICE CG31, with augmentation options held in reserve; an opioid review under the CDC 1943 guideline with a prescription drug monitoring program check, urine drug testing, naloxone, a nonjudgmental DSM-5-TR assessment that finds opioid use disorder and a switch from codeine to buprenorphine, which treats both the disorder and the pain; non-opioid pain care with physical therapy; audiometry and hearing aids for noise-induced hearing loss; weight, nutrition and kidney function; and how money and household staff can carry out compulsions for a patient and so feed avoidance, with staff involved in treatment only with his consent.
